newsitem.title: CHINA: China hopes for progress this month on WTO entry.
newsitem.headline: China hopes for progress this month on WTO entry.

text.p: China hopes to make new progress on its application to join the World Trade Organisation (WTO) in a meeting in Geneva scheduled for later this month, a foreign trade official said on Wednesday.
"We always hope for progress in such meetings," an official of the international department of the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation said by telephone.

"But China's entry will hinge on WTO members," he said, referring to the bilateral talks that lay the groundwork for accession. "We have already presented what we can offer to members and it is up to them to decide."

China has been seeking to join the world trade body on the easier terms offered developing countries, but Western nations, led by the United States, maintain its economy is too big for such preferential treatment.
A working group including China and WTO members interested in China's entry would meet later this month in Geneva to try to iron out the differences, the official said.
"We think that China's opening up of its economy has reached the level suitable for a developing country," he said.
China slashed its average import tariff to 23 percent last April from 35 percent, the biggest single cut the country has implemented. Beijing says it plans more such reductions.

However, the official dismissed as inaccurate a report in the New York Times on Wednesday that China was willing to scrap barriers, such as laws protecting some of China's state- and military-run industries from foreign competition.
"China doesn't have special laws protecting state- and military-run industries," he said. "Plus, the issue is not included in WTO talks."
He declined to give further details.

The Times said Clinton administration officials had warned that the offers had so far been conveyed in conversations only and they were wary of China's willingness to follow through with some of the changes discussed.

"There always has been a dysfunction between what they say and what they put in writing. And for WTO accession, what they put in writing is what counts," the newspaper quoted Charlene Barshefsky, the acting U.S. trade respresentative, as saying.
It quoted those involved in the talks as saying China had agreed to eliminate, over time, the requirement that foreign firms building factories in China export most of their output.
China had agreed to phase out rules requiring foreign firms to bring large amounts of foreign currency into China and to include high levels of local content for their goods, it said.
China made the agreements in a recent round of talks that were intended to preview formal negotiations that the newspaper said were scheduled to begin in Geneva on March 4.
